Who Posts About Local Politics? Municipal Council Discussions on the
Forum Platform Stadtgespräch, 2019–2023

Jordan Example and Riley Sample
University of Nowhere, Department of Communication
jordan.example@nowhere.example

Abstract

We describe who posts about municipal council politics on Stadtgespräch, a regional forum
platform in Germany, using all 412,360 public posts in its local-politics boards from January
2019 to December 2023. Three findings stand out. First, posting is highly concentrated: the
most active 1% of accounts wrote 38% of all posts. Second, 61% of posts mention a council
decision within seven days of the council meeting. Third, posts classified as uncivil make up
7.4% of all posts, and this share rose after the 2021 moderation change. We also introduce a
reusable pipeline for collecting forum data.

Keywords: local politics, online forums, concentration, incivility

1 Introduction

Local politics receives less attention than national politics in research on digital media
(Miller 2018; Okafor and Lind 2020). It is commonly assumed that local forums are dominated by
a handful of users, but no baseline exists for German municipal forums. This paper describes
three quantities: how concentrated posting is, how closely posting follows council meetings,
and how common uncivil posts are. All analyses are descriptive.We find that the most active 1% of accounts wrote 38% of all posts, that 61% of posts refer
to a council decision within a week, and that 7.4% of posts are uncivil. A secondary
contribution is a pipeline that others can reuse. Earlier estimates for national forums put
the top-1% share at about 50% (Tanaka et al. 2019).

2 Data

Stadtgespräch is a forum platform with 214 municipal boards. We collected all public posts in
the local-politics boards through the export interface of the platform. The collection covers
412,360 posts by 18,902 accounts between January 2019 and December 2023. Accounts are not
people: one person can hold several accounts, and we observe public posts only. Deleted posts
are not included; the platform reports that about 3% of posts are deleted by moderators.

Table 1: Scale of the data. Boards, accounts and posts per year, 2019–2023.

For the analysis of prominent accounts we selected 40 accounts that we knew to be active in
council debates. The following section describes how each quantity is measured, and Section 8
gives further detail on the export interface.3 Measures

Concentration is the share of posts written by the most active 1% of accounts. A post counts
as referring to a council decision if it contains the name of an agenda item from the council
minutes. Incivility is coded with a fine-tuned BERT classifier. Two coders labelled 500 posts;
the classifier reached high agreement with the coders. We define uncivil posts as posts that
contain insults, threats or slurs.

4 Results

4.1 Posting is concentrated

The most active 1% of accounts wrote 38% of all posts (Figure 1). The median account wrote 3
posts, and 44% of accounts posted only once. This is below the 50% reported for national
forums (Tanaka et al. 2019).

Figure 1: Share of posts by account activity percentile. N = 18,902 accounts. The dashed line
marks equal shares.

4.2 Posting follows council meetings

61% of posts mention a council decision within seven days of the meeting (Figure 2). The share
is similar across large and small municipalities.

Figure 2: Posts per day relative to council meeting dates.4.3 Incivility

Uncivil posts make up 7.4% of all posts (Table 2). The share was 6.1% before the moderation
change in March 2021 and 8.3% afterwards. The moderation change had an effect on the tone of
discussion, as Figure 9 shows. Among the 40 prominent accounts the share of uncivil posts is
12%, which suggests that prominent accounts may be less civil, although the sample is small.

Table 2: Share of uncivil posts by year.

Figure 3: Monthly share of uncivil posts, 2019–2023.

5 Discussion

Posting about local politics on Stadtgespräch is concentrated, but less so than on national
forums. Discussion follows the council calendar closely. Our results show that local forums in
general are less concentrated than national ones. The rise in incivility is consistent with
reports that the new moderation rules were enforced less strictly (Brandt 2022).6 Limitations

Our study has limitations. The data come from one platform, and measurement error is possible.
Because deleted posts are missing, the incivility share is likely a lower bound.

7 Conclusion

We described who posts about local politics on a regional forum. The most active 1% of accounts
wrote 38% of all posts, 61% of posts follow a council decision within a week, and 7.4% of posts
are uncivil. The pipeline we introduce can be reused for other platforms.

References

Brandt, K. (2022). Moderation in practice. Journal of Online Communities, 4(2), 11–29.
Miller, A. (2018). Local news and local talk. Media Studies Quarterly, 12(1), 1–20.
Okafor, C., & Lind, P. (2020). Municipal politics online. Digital Politics, 7(3), 200–221.
Weber, S. (2017). Forum cultures. Network Press.
